strengths: First method to bring sliced Wasserstein distance to the streaming setting, filling a clear and practically motivated gap relative to existing streaming/online OT works (Online Sinkhorn, Compressed Online Sinkhorn), which the paper argues are too computationally expensive or scale poorly with dimension.

Solid theoretical development: probabilistic (Hoeffding-type) bounds on the error of streaming CDF and quantile-function estimates via KKL sketches are derived and then propagated cleanly through 1D Wasserstein distance, the transport map, Stream-SW with population-level distributions, and the finite-projection Monte Carlo estimator (Propositions 1-4, Corollary 1, Theorem 1), giving a coherent end-to-end guarantee chain.

Careful complexity analysis showing space complexity logarithmic in stream length n and linear in sketch size k, and near-linear time complexity, which is the central practical selling point for memory-constrained/streaming applications.

Reasonably broad empirical validation: controlled approximation-error studies on Gaussians/GMMs and MNIST, plus three different downstream tasks (point-cloud KNN classification, gradient flows, streaming change-point detection), consistently showing Stream-SW outperforms a random-subsampling baseline at matched or lower memory budgets.

Additional runtime scalability experiment (Appendix C, Table 7) demonstrates Stream-SW remains tractable at millions of streamed points where full SW runs out of memory and naive random-sampling SW becomes very slow.
weaknesses: The only empirical baseline is random subsampling; there is no empirical comparison against other streaming quantile sketches (e.g., Greenwald-Khanna, t-digest) or against the Compressed Online Sinkhorn method that motivates the paper in the introduction, making it hard to judge how much of the benefit is specific to KKL sketches versus sketching in general, or how Stream-SW compares to existing streaming OT baselines in practice.

The finite-sample theoretical guarantees (Propositions 1-4, Theorem 1) rely on a compact-support assumption with constants depending on the diameter R (and on p, a) that are not made explicit or bounded with respect to dimension d; this creates a gap with the experiments, which include unbounded Gaussian distributions not satisfying the stated assumption.

The framework treats the two distributions µ, ν as fixed and draws i.i.d. streaming samples from them; genuine non-stationary/streaming phenomena (concept drift, evolving distributions over time) are not modeled or theoretically analyzed, which somewhat undercuts the applicability claims for tasks like change-point detection where the underlying premise is that distributions do change over time.

Despite emphasizing that KKL sketches are mergeable and thus suitable for distributed computation, no experiments actually test distributed/merged sketch computation; this claimed advantage is untested.

The change-point detection experiment (Section 4.4) is reported as single delay values per subject (Table 3) without repeated trials, confidence intervals, or sensitivity analysis to threshold/bootstrap choices, limiting confidence in the robustness of this result.

Presentation is dense with heavy notation and could better delineate assumptions (e.g., compact support) needed for each theoretical result versus what is used in experiments; some appendix tables (e.g., Table 6 with variable "M") are not clearly cross-referenced/defined in the main text.

All experiments are run on a single desktop machine with implementation noted as unoptimized pure Python for the sketch/compaction step, so the reported wall-clock comparisons (Table 7) may not reflect achievable performance with optimized implementations, and no comparison of implementation efficiency against optimized OT/Sinkhorn libraries is given.

strengths: The paper addresses a legitimate and underexplored problem (computing sliced Wasserstein distance from streaming data with bounded memory), which is practically relevant for IoT/streaming applications.

The theoretical development is thorough for what it is: Propositions 1-4, Corollary 1 and Theorem 1 provide concentration bounds relating the streaming (KKL-sketch-based) CDF/quantile/1DW/Stream-SW estimators to their empirical and population counterparts, with proofs given in the appendix.
Complexity analysis (space logarithmic in n, linear in sketch size k; time near-linear in n and k) is explicitly derived and clearly presented.

The experimental suite is reasonably broad, covering synthetic Gaussian/GMM comparisons, point-cloud classification, gradient flows, and change-point detection, giving some sense of applicability across tasks.
The writing and organization are generally clear, and the connection between 1D quantile-based OT and streaming quantile sketches is a sensible, well-explained design choice.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is a fairly direct combination of two existing, well-established components — the KKL streaming quantile sketch (Karnin et al., 2016) and the standard quantile-function-based closed form of 1D Wasserstein/SW distance — with the theoretical proofs mostly following from standard tools (Hoeffding, DKW inequality, union bounds) rather than presenting substantially new proof techniques.

Despite extensively motivating the work by contrasting with Online Sinkhorn and Compressed Online Sinkhorn as the main existing streaming OT approaches, the paper never empirically compares Stream-SW against either method; all empirical comparisons are against a weak random-subsampling baseline, leaving the central practical claim (Stream-SW is better than existing streaming OT solutions) empirically unverified.

No comparison is made against other streaming quantile summary structures (e.g., Greenwald-Khanna, t-digest) mentioned in the introduction, despite the choice of KKL sketch being presented as a design decision worth justifying empirically.

The change-point detection experiment compares Stream-SW (which uses the full observed history) against a fixed-window sliding baseline; these differ in more than just the streaming quantile approximation (i.e., in how much data/context each uses), confounding the source of the reported improvement. Results also lack repeated trials/error bars (Table 3) despite variance being reported elsewhere in the paper.

In the point-cloud classification experiment, Stream-SW sometimes outperforms Full SW (which retains all data), which is counterintuitive and warrants deeper investigation or explanation (e.g., regularization/denoising effect); as presented, with no reported variance over multiple runs, this could reflect noise rather than a genuine effect.

The computational time comparisons (Table 7) pit a GPU/PyTorch-optimized Full SW implementation against an admittedly unoptimized pure-Python Stream-SW implementation, making the reported runtime advantages of Stream-SW at large n only partially informative about real-world computational efficiency.

Several theoretical guarantees assume compact support with diameter R, which is violated in the Gaussian/GMM experiments used to validate the approach; while the authors acknowledge this as a complement to theory, it somewhat weakens the direct empirical support for the compact-support bounds.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and practically relevant gap: no prior streaming estimator for sliced Wasserstein distance existed, and the paper provides the first such method with a clean derivation route (streaming CDF/quantile estimation via KKL sketches -> streaming 1D Wasserstein -> Stream-SW).

Strong theoretical backing: the paper provides non-trivial probabilistic approximation guarantees for streaming CDF estimation (Prop. 1), streaming quantile estimation (Prop. 2), streaming 1D Wasserstein and transport maps (Props. 3-4), and extends these through Corollary 1 and Theorem 1 to Stream-SW with finite projections, with full proofs given in the appendix.
Careful complexity analysis showing Stream-SW achieves logarithmic-in-n space complexity and near-linear time complexity, directly explaining the practical memory savings observed empirically.

Broad and diverse empirical validation: synthetic Gaussian/GMM comparisons, MNIST digit comparisons, point-cloud classification (ModelNet10), point-cloud gradient flows (ShapeNet), and streaming change-point detection (MSRC-12 Kinect gestures), consistently showing Stream-SW outperforms naive random-subsampling SW at matched memory budgets.

Scalability experiment (Appendix C, Table 7) convincingly demonstrates the practical value of the approach: full SW runs out of memory at 2M points while Stream-SW remains tractable, and the random-sampling baseline becomes prohibitively slow at large k, highlighting Stream-SW's advantage.

The paper is well organized, clearly explains the connection between streaming quantile sketches and the quantile-function-based closed form of 1D Wasserstein distance, and includes ablations over sketch size k and stream length n that support the stated theoretical trends.
weaknesses: The core streaming quantile data structure (KKL sketch) is borrowed directly from prior work (Karnin et al., 2016); the main novelty lies in coupling it with the SW/1DW quantile representation and re-deriving guarantees, which is a solid but somewhat incremental technical contribution rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea.

The only streaming baseline compared throughout is naive random subsampling with a matched memory budget; other streaming quantile sketches (e.g., GK, t-digest, DDSketch) or alternative memory-constrained strategies for SW estimation are not benchmarked, making it harder to assess how much of the improvement is specific to the KKL choice versus streaming sketches in general.

Several theoretical guarantees (Props. 1-4, Theorem 1) rely on compact-support assumptions; while the empirical Gaussian experiments partially address the non-compact case, the paper does not derive matching rates for unbounded-support distributions, leaving a gap between theory and some experimental settings.

Reported runtimes are explicitly noted to be from a pure Python, non-optimized, non-parallelized implementation, which weakens the practical significance of the computational-time comparisons presented in the appendix (though the trend/scalability argument is still informative).

The point-cloud classification results (Table 2) show that Stream-SW's advantage shrinks and becomes only comparable to (not clearly better than) full SW/random sampling once k is moderately large, suggesting the benefit is most pronounced only in the very low-memory regime.

Limitations such as behavior under non-stationary or adversarially ordered streams, or heavy-tailed distributions where sketch-based quantile approximation may degrade, are not discussed or empirically tested.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and previously unexplored problem: extending sliced Wasserstein (SW) distance computation to the streaming setting, where existing methods (Online Sinkhorn, Compressed Online Sinkhorn) are shown to be memory- or computation-inefficient.

The theoretical development is thorough and self-consistent: probabilistic guarantees are established sequentially for streaming CDF estimation, streaming quantile function estimation, streaming 1D Wasserstein distance, the corresponding transport map, and finally Stream-SW itself (via projection), with both empirical-to-empirical and empirical-to-population bounds.

Complexity analysis is explicit and favorable: space complexity logarithmic in stream length n and linear in sketch size k, with near-linear time complexity, which is a meaningful practical advantage over prior streaming OT methods.

Diverse empirical evaluation spanning synthetic Gaussian/Gaussian-mixture comparisons, MNIST digit comparison, point-cloud classification (ModelNet10), gradient flows (ShapeNet), and streaming change-point detection (MSRC-12 Kinect), which supports the general applicability of the method.
Additional practical extensions are provided (one-sided Stream-SW, gradient approximation for parametric distributions), increasing usability for downstream tasks like generative modeling.
Reasonably transparent complexity/runtime study (Appendix, Table 7) showing scalability to millions of samples where full SW becomes infeasible on GPU.
weaknesses: The core data structure (KLL sketch) is adopted wholesale from prior streaming-quantile literature (Karnin et al., 2016); the main novelty is combining it with the well-known quantile-based formula for 1D Wasserstein distance and slicing, which is a fairly direct/incremental combination rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea.

The only empirical baseline is naive random subsampling; the paper does not empirically compare against Online Sinkhorn, Compressed Online Sinkhorn, or other streaming quantile sketches (e.g., Greenwald-Khanna, t-digest), despite motivating the work by critiquing these methods in the introduction.

Several of the tightest theoretical results (uniform CDF/quantile bounds, Proposition 3's better rates) rely on a compact-support assumption; guarantees for unbounded distributions are comparatively weaker/pointwise only, limiting applicability to heavy-tailed or genuinely unbounded streaming data.

The reported implementation for Stream-SW and the sampling baseline is 'pure Python without optimized libraries or parallelization' (Appendix C), which undermines the reliability of the runtime comparisons and makes the wall-clock scalability claims less convincing until validated with optimized implementations.

The change-point detection experiment's methodology (fixed window size for baseline, choice of thresholding, bootstrap procedure) is only briefly described, and only one dataset (MSRC-12) is used, limiting the strength of the claimed advantage over sliding-window methods.

Some constants in the theoretical bounds (Ap,R, Cp,R, etc.) are not explicitly characterized in terms of dimension d or p, and the dependence of the guarantees on d is not discussed despite d being central to the motivation (curse of dimensionality).

strengths: Addresses a genuine, previously unexplored gap: no prior streaming estimator existed for sliced Wasserstein distance, despite streaming entropic OT (Online Sinkhorn, Compressed Online Sinkhorn) already being studied.
The connection between 1D Wasserstein's closed-form quantile representation and streaming quantile sketches (KLL) is a natural and reasonably elegant way to construct the estimator.

A fairly complete theoretical package is provided: concentration bounds for streaming CDF/quantile estimation, propagation of these bounds to 1D Wasserstein and the associated transport map, and further propagation to Stream-SW (finite-projection MC estimator included), together with a space/time complexity analysis.

The empirical evaluation spans several settings (parametric Gaussian/GMM comparison with closed-form ground truth, MNIST, point-cloud classification, gradient flows, and change-point detection), giving some breadth to the validation.
Reported memory/accuracy trade-off curves and runtime tables (Appendix C) show Stream-SW dominates naive random subsampling at matched memory budgets in the tested regimes.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core idea is to plug an existing, off-the-shelf streaming quantile sketch (KLL, Karnin et al. 2016) into the already-known quantile-function formula for 1D/sliced Wasserstein. Proposition 1 largely re-derives known KLL concentration guarantees, and Propositions 2-4/Corollary 1/Theorem 1 follow by fairly mechanical triangle-inequality and Lipschitz arguments (mean value theorem, DKW, Hoeffding). The conceptual leap beyond 'apply known sketch + known SW formula' is modest.

The only baseline compared throughout is 'SW with random subsampling at equal memory,' which is a weak strawman; no comparison is made to other streaming quantile sketches (e.g., Greenwald-Khanna, t-digest, reservoir sampling with better allocation) or to the streaming OT baselines discussed at length in the introduction (Online Sinkhorn, Compressed Online Sinkhorn), even though those are explicitly positioned as the motivating prior work.

Theory is stated for compactly supported distributions of diameter R, yet the main simulation study (Section 4.1) explicitly uses unbounded Gaussians and Gaussian mixtures, so the reported experiments are not actually covered by the stated theorems; the paper does not supply a corresponding non-compact-support guarantee or clearly justify the extrapolation.

The streaming change-point detection experiment's baseline (sliding-window SW) appears to be a weak/underspecified comparator (fixed window size 100, very large reported detection delays for several subjects, e.g., 100/100/49/100 for the baseline), raising questions about whether the comparison is fair or whether the baseline was properly tuned.

Several quantitative results have limited or ambiguous practical significance: e.g., Table 4/5 show the Stream-SW vs. random-sampling gap shrinking substantially as k or n grow, and in Table 5 at n=2000 random sampling even slightly outperforms Stream-SW, undercutting the claimed general superiority.

Complexity analysis is purely asymptotic/theoretical; the appendix runtime table itself notes the streaming implementation is unoptimized pure Python, making the practical runtime comparisons (e.g., vs. GPU-based full SW) not very informative about real-world deployment costs on IoT/streaming hardware, which is the paper's stated motivating scenario.

The paper does not discuss failure modes, sensitivity to the arbitrary/adversarial ordering of streamed samples (only i.i.d. stream order seems implicitly assumed in the theory), or how performance degrades under distribution shift within the stream, which is central to realistic streaming applications.

strengths: Addresses a novel and well-motivated problem: the paper is the first to propose a streaming estimator for sliced Wasserstein distance, an important gap given the increasing need for memory-constrained streaming distance computation (e.g., IoT applications).

Strong theoretical contribution: the paper provides a thorough chain of probabilistic approximation guarantees, from streaming CDF/quantile estimation (Propositions 1-2) through streaming 1DW (Proposition 3) and its associated transport map (Proposition 4), up to Stream-SW itself (Corollary 1, Theorem 1), with detailed and largely self-contained proofs in the appendix.

Clear complexity analysis showing Stream-SW achieves logarithmic space complexity in the stream length n and near-linear time complexity, which is a meaningful practical advantage over prior streaming OT approaches like Online/Compressed Online Sinkhorn discussed in the introduction.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning synthetic distribution comparison (Gaussians, Gaussian mixtures, MNIST), point-cloud classification, point-cloud gradient flows, and streaming change-point detection, consistently showing Stream-SW outperforms naive random-sampling baselines in accuracy and/or memory usage.

Good transparency in reporting runtime results (Table 7), including honest acknowledgment that the implementation is unoptimized pure Python and that further speedups are possible, and additional ablations (varying n, k, L) supporting the theoretical trends.
weaknesses: The empirical comparisons are limited to SW with random subsampling; despite extensively motivating the work against Online Sinkhorn and Compressed Online Sinkhorn in the introduction, no direct empirical comparison against these (or other) streaming/online OT baselines is provided, making it hard to assess practical advantages over existing streaming OT methods.

The streaming setting in most experiments (point-cloud classification, gradient flow, MNIST, ModelNet, ShapeNet) is synthetically constructed by feeding static datasets through a stream in an ad hoc manner rather than using genuinely streaming/online data sources, which somewhat limits the practical realism of the evaluation.

Theoretical guarantees rely on compact support assumptions (diameter R); the non-compact case (e.g., unbounded Gaussians used in the main simulation) is only validated empirically, and no theoretical treatment or discussion of how the bounds degrade or transfer to unbounded-support distributions is given.

The change-point detection experiment setup and the resulting Table 3/Figure 5 comparison could be described more rigorously (e.g., clarity on how thresholds/null distributions are constructed and why Stream-SW is expected to yield systematically lower detection delay beyond memory savings) to strengthen the significance claims for that application.

Only a single desktop machine is reported for all experiments with limited details on hyperparameter selection, random seeds, and variance sources in the main text (details are relegated to the appendix), which somewhat limits reproducibility from the main paper alone.

The paper's dense notation and heavy reliance on sequential propositions/corollaries (Propositions 1-4, Corollary 1, Theorem 1) makes the presentation demanding to follow, and could benefit from more intuition or a summary figure connecting the pieces before diving into individual proofs.
